answer.headline: SFO arrival delays sit above the US pool, with higher NAS minutes and lower weather-cause minutes
answer.body:
These values are calculated from domestic On-Time arrivals over {F1.period}, the default trailing twelve months. They are not forecasts or estimates.

San Francisco International (SFO) had an arrival delay rate of {F1}. The arrival-weighted pool of US airports in the commercial enplanement group was {F4}. The absolute gap in the rate (SFO minus that pool) is {F10}. Relative to the pool, SFO is {F11} higher.

NAS (airspace and system) delay minutes per arrival were {F2} at SFO and {F5} in that pool. The absolute gap is {F12}. The relative gap is {F13}.

Weather delay minutes per arrival were {F3} at SFO and {F6} in the pool. SFO is lower on this category: the absolute gap is {F14} and the relative gap is {F15}.

The same pattern appears against FAA large hubs, so the gap is not only a contrast with smaller airports. The large-hub arrival delay rate is {F7} (SFO gap {F16}). Large-hub NAS minutes per arrival are {F8} (absolute gap {F17}, relative gap {F18}). Large-hub weather minutes per arrival are {F9} (SFO gap {F19}).

The data do not establish why SFO is delayed. The higher arrival delay rate coincides with higher NAS minutes per arrival, and it does not coincide with higher weather-cause minutes. That is a comparison of recorded delay-cause categories, not a physical cause.

claims.text: Over {F1.period}, the SFO arrival delay rate was {F1}, versus {F4} for the arrival-weighted US commercial pool.
The absolute gap in that rate (SFO minus the pool) is {F10}. Relative to the pool, SFO is {F11} higher.
SFO NAS delay minutes per arrival were {F2}, versus {F5} in the US commercial pool. The absolute gap is {F12} and the relative gap is {F13}.
SFO weather delay minutes per arrival were {F3}, versus {F6} in the US commercial pool. The absolute gap is {F14} and the relative gap is {F15}. SFO is below the pool on weather-cause minutes.

Versus FAA large hubs, the arrival delay rate is {F7} (SFO gap {F16}), NAS minutes per arrival are {F8} (absolute gap {F17}, relative gap {F18}), and weather minutes per arrival are {F9} (SFO gap {F19}).

The elevated arrival delay rate lines up with elevated NAS (airspace and system) minutes per arrival. It does not line up with elevated weather-cause minutes, which are lower at SFO than in both pools. This describes which recorded category is high. It does not identify a meteorological, capacity, or demand cause.

assumptions: SFO is San Francisco International Airport, the unique airport match for that code.
National average means the arrival-weighted group total of each metric (a ratio of sums across airports), not the unweighted mean of airport-level rates.
The national set is US airports passing the catalog commercial enplanement group filter. An unrestricted US airport set was rejected as too large to aggregate.
Both pools include SFO, so each gap compares SFO with a benchmark that already contains SFO.
Large-hub results are a peer check using the FAA large-hub class. They are not the national average.
The window is the default trailing twelve months of On-Time data, {F1.period}.
limitations: A cause of the delays is not established. Unmet demand, terminal capacity, fares, and profitability are not measured by these metrics.

NAS minutes are airspace and system delay minutes per operated arrival. Weather minutes are the weather delay-cause category per operated arrival. Neither is a weather observation, a runway-capacity measure, or a forecast.
Carrier delay, late-aircraft delay, and security delay are not catalog metrics, so this is not a full delay-cause decomposition.

On-Time covers domestic flights of reporting carriers only, so international flights and smaller carriers are excluded. That scope matters at SFO. The low-coverage caveat was not attached. Coverage is computed on months shared with T-100, which does not include every month of the On-Time window.
Results are a descriptive comparison. They are not a screening rank and not a valuation.
